besanosaurus:enwiki:7.title: Besanosaurus (Putative specimens from Svalbard and Germany, part 2)

facts.statement: The genus Besanosaurus was named by Cristiano Dal Sasso and Giovanni Pinna in 1996.
facts.quote: authority: Dal Sasso & Pinna, 1996

facts.statement: Besanosaurus lived during the Middle Triassic, specifically the latest Anisian stage.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Middle Triassic, latest Anisian,

facts.statement: Besanosaurus is an extinct genus of ichthyosaur found in the Monte San Giorgio region of Italy and Switzerland.
facts.quote: Besanosaurus (meaning reptile from Besano) is an extinct genus of Middle Triassic ichthyosaur from Monte San Giorgio of Italy and Switzerland

facts.statement: The genus Besanosaurus contains only one known species, B. leptorhynchus.
facts.quote: containing the single species B. leptorhynchus

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Besanosaurus is the nearly complete flattened skeleton designated BES SC 999.
facts.quote: based on the nearly complete flattened skeleton BES SC 999, the holotype specimen

facts.statement: Specimens previously classified as separate genera, such as Mikadocephalus, have been reinterpreted as belonging to Besanosaurus.
facts.quote: Additional specimens from Monte San Giorgio that have previously been considered separate genera, including a partial skull named Mikadocephalus and a well-preserved, largely complete skeleton, have been reinterpreted as additional specimens of Besanosaurus

facts.statement: Putative specimens of Besanosaurus have been found in Svalbard and Germany, but their classification remains disputed.
facts.quote: Putative specimens have been discovered in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard and Germany, although their attribution to the genus remains disputed

facts.statement: The largest known specimen of Besanosaurus is estimated to be about 8 meters long.
facts.quote: Besanosaurus is a large ichthyosaur, with the largest known specimen estimated to measure about 8 m long

facts.statement: Besanosaurus had a long, slender body characterized by a small head and a long tail.
facts.quote: It has a long, slender body with a small head and long tail

facts.statement: Besanosaurus possessed a long, thin snout containing numerous small, pointed teeth.
facts.quote: The snout of Besanosaurus is long and thin, and contains numerous small pointed teeth

facts.statement: In the upper jaw of Besanosaurus, most teeth were set in sockets while the rearmost teeth were implanted in a groove.
facts.quote: In the upper jaw, the teeth are mostly set into sockets but the rearmost teeth are implanted in a groove

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Besanosaurus featured enlarged coronoid processes used to anchor jaw muscles.
facts.quote: The lower jaw bears enlarged coronoid processes for the anchorage of jaw muscles

facts.statement: The tail of Besanosaurus comprised more than half of its total length and exhibited a downward bend.
facts.quote: The tail made up more than half the animal's length and displays a downward bend

facts.statement: Besanosaurus had forelimbs longer than its hindlimbs, with round and squat humeri.
facts.quote: The forelimbs are longer than the hindlimbs, and the humeri are round and squat

facts.statement: It is unclear exactly how Besanosaurus and other shastasaurid ichthyosaurs are related to one another.
facts.quote: While it is understood to be a shastasaurid-type ichthyosaur, how exactly Besanosaurus and other members of this group are related to each other is unclear

facts.statement: Strong jaw muscles and a delicate snout suggest Besanosaurus fed on small fish and coleoid cephalopods using rapid, snapping bites.
facts.quote: The skull bones of Besanosaurus indicate that it would have possessed strong jaw muscles, but its delicate snout suggests it would have fed on small fish and coleoid cephalopods, which it could have caught with rapid, snapping bites

facts.statement: All definite specimens of Besanosaurus originate from the Besano Formation.
facts.quote: All definite specimens of Besanosaurus come from the Besano Formation

facts.statement: During the Anisian, the region of the Besano Formation was a lagoon populated by diverse marine life, including other ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: During the Anisian, this region was a lagoon populated by a wide variety of marine life, including a variety of other ichthyosaurs

facts.statement: Paleontological work at the Sasso Caldo site on the Italian side of Monte San Giorgio began in 1985.
facts.quote: In 1985, paleontological work began at a site known as Sasso Caldo (meaning warm stone) on the Italian side of Monte San Giorgio

facts.statement: The excavation at Sasso Caldo was the longest-lasting excavation conducted at Monte San Giorgio.
facts.quote: The excavation at Sasso Caldo is the longest-lasting excavation that was conducted at Monte San Giorgio

facts.statement: In spring 1993, a piece of shale containing parts of a large ichthyosaur's jaws broke loose during excavation.
facts.quote: In the spring of 1993, while extracting a block of dolomite containing the skeletons of a pair of mixosaurid ichthyosaurs, a piece of shale from the layer below broke loose

facts.statement: By February 1996, approximately 2,500 hours of preparation had been performed on the Besanosaurus holotype.
facts.quote: By February 1996, 2500 hours of preparation had been performed by three or four preparators on the specimen

facts.statement: Dal Sasso and Pinna designated the specimen as the holotype of the new genus and species Besanosaurus leptorhynchus due to its differences from other shastasaurs.
facts.quote: Dal Sasso and Pinna found the specimen to differ from other shastasaurs, and made it the holotype of a new genus and species, Besanosaurus leptorhynchus

facts.statement: Some researchers suggested in 1998 that Besanosaurus might represent another specimen of Shastasaurus, though it is generally accepted as a valid taxon.
facts.quote: While P. Martin Sander and Christiane Faber in 1998 considered it possible that Besanosaurus represented another specimen of the related Shastasaurus, Besanosaurus has otherwise been accepted as a valid taxon

facts.statement: The holotype of Besanosaurus was not the first shastasaurid specimen discovered in Monte San Giorgio.
facts.quote: The holotype of Besanosaurus was not the first shastasaur known from Monte San Giorgio.

facts.statement: Two shastasaurid specimens from Switzerland were deposited in the collections of the Paläontologisches Institut und Museum der Universität Zürich in the 1920s.
facts.quote: Two shastasaurid specimens from Switzerland were deposited in the collections of Paläontologisches Institut und Museum der Universität Zürich in the 1920s

facts.statement: Specimen PIMUZ T 4847 is a very large, poorly preserved, and disarticulated skeleton missing the tail and limbs, recovered from layer 116 of the Cava Tre Fontane mine.
facts.quote: The other specimen, hailing from layer 116 of the Cava Tre Fontane mine, is cataloged as PIMUZ T 4847 and is very large, and poorly preserved and disarticulated, missing the tail and limbs.

facts.statement: In 1993, Sander and Jean Michel Mazin considered both shastasaurid specimens to represent distinct genera.
facts.quote: Sander and Jean Michel Mazin considered both of these specimens to represent a distinct genera in 1993.

facts.statement: David Cook published an abstract in 1994 interpreting the medium-sized specimen as pertaining to a new genus.
facts.quote: The medium-sized specimen was studied by David Cook, who had an abstract published in 1994, in which this specimen was interpreted as pertaining to a new genus.

facts.statement: In 1997, Michael Maisch and Andreas Matzke described an ichthyosaur skull cataloged as GPIT 1793/1 housed at the Palaeontological Collection of Tübingen University.
facts.quote: In 1997, Michael Maisch and Andreas Matzke described an ichthyosaur skull housed at the Palaeontological Collection of Tübingen University, cataloged as GPIT 1793/1.

facts.statement: Maisch and Matzke named the skull specimen the holotype of the new genus and species Mikadocephalus gracilirostris.
facts.quote: Maisch and Matzke named it the holotype of a new genus and species, Mikadocephalus gracilirostris.

facts.statement: Maisch and Matzke referred specimen PIMUZ T 4376 to M. gracilirostris and assigned specimen PIMUZ T 1895 to Besanosaurus.
facts.quote: Additionally, they referred PIMUZ T 4376 to M. gracilirostris, and assigned another specimen to Besanosaurus, PIMUZ T 1895.

facts.statement: In a 2003 book, Christopher McGowan and Ryosuke Motani listed both M. gracilirostris and Wimanius odontopalatus as species inquirendae.
facts.quote: In a 2003 book, Christopher McGowan and Ryosuke Motani listed both M. gracilirostris and Wimanius odontopalatus as a species inquirendae

facts.statement: The first remains of Besanosaurus consisted of 11 vertebrae and some rib fragments discovered in the 1860s.
facts.quote: The first remains of this taxon were a total of 11 vertebrae with some associated rib fragments found during the 1860s

facts.statement: John Hulke named the initial remains Ichthyosaurus polaris in 1873.
facts.quote: named Ichthyosaurus polaris by John Hulke in 1873

facts.statement: Carl Wiman established the genus Pessosaurus to contain the species.
facts.quote: Carl Wiman named a new genus, Pessosaurus, to contain the species

facts.statement: Maisch and Matzke agreed in 2000 with the view that Pessosaurus was a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: Maisch and Matzke in 2000 agreed with the taxonomic position of Sander and Faber

facts.statement: Bindellini and colleagues found in 2024 that the similar femur anatomy between PIMUZ T 4376 and Pessosaurus resulted from incomplete fossils.
facts.quote: In 2024, Bindellini and colleagues determined that the similar femur anatomy of PIMUZ T 4376 and Pessosaurus was the result of the femora being incomplete

facts.statement: Bindellini and colleagues concluded in 2024 that there is no evidence of Besanosaurus from Svalbard.
facts.quote: Bindellini and colleagues in 2024 also considered Pessopteryx to be distinct from Besanosaurus, and concluded that there was no evidence of Besanosaurus from Svalbard

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene described Pessosaurus suevicus in 1916 based on a single vertebra from the Black Forest in Germany.
facts.quote: In 1916, Friedrich von Huene erected a second species of Pessosaurus, P. suevicus, on the basis of a single vertebra discovered in the Muschelkalk of the Black Forest in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany

facts.statement: Besanosaurus had an elongate body shape resembling Cymbospondylus.
facts.quote: Besanosaurus is more elongate, and resembles Cymbospondylus in overall shape

facts.statement: About half of the total length of Besanosaurus was formed by its very long tail.
facts.quote: In addition to having an elongate trunk, about half of the total length of Besanosaurus is formed by its very long tail

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Besanosaurus measured 5.065 meters in length.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen measures 5.065 m long from its snout tip to tail tip

facts.statement: The largest known specimen of Besanosaurus, PIMUZ T 4847, was estimated at 8 meters long, making it the largest known ichthyosaur in its environment.
facts.quote: The specimen PIMUZ T 4847 was estimated by Bindellini and colleagues in 2021 to have a total length of 8 m, and is the largest known specimen of Besanosaurus, indicating that Besanosaurus is the largest known ichthyosaur in its environment

facts.statement: Besanosaurus lived in the Upper Saurian Niveau of Svalbard from the Ladinian to the Carnian stages of the Triassic.
facts.quote: Historically, a fairly rare species of large ichthyosaur was reported from the units informally termed the "Upper Saurian Niveau" of Svalbard, spanning from the Ladinian stage of the Middle Triassic to the Carnian stage of the Late Triassic

facts.statement: Maisch argued in 2010 that Pessopteryx and Besanosaurus were not close relatives and showed various differences.
facts.quote: Maisch, however, in 2010, argued against this synonymy, noting that his previous publications with Matzke had found various differences between Pessopteryx and Besanosaurus, and recovered the two of them as not being particularly close relatives

facts.statement: Maxwell and Kear agreed in 2013 that Pessopteryx was distinct from Besanosaurus, though they doubted some material assignments.
facts.quote: Maxwell and Kear in 2013 doubted the assignment of some of the material considered to be Pessopteryx by Maisch and Matzke, but agreed that it was distinct from Besanosaurus

facts.statement: The skull of Besanosaurus is dominated by a very long, thin snout that contains small teeth.
facts.quote: About two-thirds of the skull of Besanosaurus is occupied by its very long, thin snout lined with small teeth.

facts.statement: Well-preserved skulls reveal that Besanosaurus had long, slot-like openings for its nostrils.
facts.quote: Well-preserved Besanosaurus skulls show drawn-out slotlike external nares, openings which housed the nostrils in life.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus possessed scleral rings made of 15 to 17 bony plates to support its eyes.
facts.quote: Within the orbits are the scleral rings, circles of bony, quadrangular plates that supported the eyeballs. Bindellini and colleagues estimated a total of between 15 and 17 of these plates per ring in Besanosaurus.

facts.statement: The back region of the Besanosaurus skull is short, making up 13% of the skull's total length.
facts.quote: The region behind the orbits is short, occupying 13% of the skull's length, though it is still long compared to some parvipelvians.

facts.statement: The frontals in Besanosaurus are long, broad, and flat bones that form the supratemporal terraces but do not border the fenestrae.
facts.quote: The frontals are long, broad, and flat bones involved in the supratemporal terraces, though they do not form any part of the borders of the supratemporal fenestrae.

facts.statement: The jugal bones of Besanosaurus are thin, strip-like structures bent at right angles.
facts.quote: The jugals are thin, strip-like bones bent at right angles.

facts.statement: Weak articulations caused the thin jugal bones of Besanosaurus to frequently separate from the skull during fossilization.
facts.quote: The articulations with other bones holding it in place were rather weak, and resultingly the jugals were often disarticulated from the skull during fossilization.

facts.statement: The jaw joint of Besanosaurus was formed by robust, kidney-shaped quadrate bones.
facts.quote: The jaw joint was formed by the robust, kidney-shaped quadrates in the cranium.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Besanosaurus is primarily formed by long, thin dentary bones that bear teeth.
facts.quote: Most of the lower jaw is formed by the long, thin toothbearing dentaries.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus has a massive coronoid process, which is only as large as that found in Phantomosaurus.
facts.quote: The coronoid process is massive in Besanosaurus, only rivaled in its development by that of Phantomosaurus.

facts.statement: All teeth of Besanosaurus are small, cone-shaped, and sharply pointed.
facts.quote: The teeth of Besanosaurus are all similar in shape, being small, cone-shaped, and acutely pointed.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus teeth have vertical ridges on their crowns and even stronger ridges on their roots, but lack cutting edges.
facts.quote: The tooth crowns are lined with vertical ridges, though lack cutting edges, while the tooth roots bear even stronger ridging.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus teeth are widely spaced and interlock when the jaws are closed.
facts.quote: The teeth are separated from each other by a rather wide amount of space and interlock when the jaw is closed.

facts.statement: Most upper jaw teeth of Besanosaurus are socketed, except for the rear 30% which are implanted in a groove.
facts.quote: Throughout most of the upper jaw, the teeth are set into sockets, with the exception of the rear 30% of the maxillary teeth, which are implanted in a groove.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Besanosaurus contains 201 vertebrae, with 61 positioned before the hips.
facts.quote: The holotype of Besanosaurus preserves 201 vertebrae, 61 of which are located in front of the hips.

facts.statement: The tail of the holotype accounts for more than half of the animal's total length and consists of at least 138 vertebrae.
facts.quote: The tail of the holotype makes up more than half of the animal's length and contains at least 138 vertebrae.

facts.statement: A separate fossil, PIMUZ T 1895, shows that the tail of Besanosaurus had a bend of approximately 30 degrees.
facts.quote: PIMUZ T 1895 preserves five wedge-shaped caudal centra, which formed an approximately 30° bend in the tail.

facts.statement: Researchers identified the location of the tail bend in Besanosaurus as occurring between the 56th and 60th tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: Bindellini and colleagues identified the tail bend as occurring from the 56th to 60th tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: The hindlimbs of Besanosaurus are approximately 70% the length of its forelimbs.
facts.quote: The hindlimbs of Besanosaurus are roughly 70% the length of its forelimbs.

facts.statement: Each forelimb of Besanosaurus has five digits, comprising the second through fifth fingers plus an additional accessory digit.
facts.quote: There are five digits in each forelimb, corresponding to the second to fifth fingers and an additional accessory digit behind them.

facts.statement: Each hindlimb of Besanosaurus possesses only four digits, corresponding to the second through fifth toes.
facts.quote: There are only four digits in each hindlimb, corresponding to the second to fifth toes.

facts.statement: The well-spaced finger bones in the forelimbs suggest that extensive cartilage was present in these limbs when the animal was alive.
facts.quote: The phalanges in the forelimb are well-spaced, indicating that extensive cartilage was present in the forelimbs during life.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus is generally classified as a shastasaurid, though its exact relationship to other members of the group remains unclear.
facts.quote: Besanosaurus has generally been considered a shastasaurid, how it is related to other shastasaurids is unclear due to the poorly understood phylogeny of the group.

facts.statement: Early phylogenetic analysis placed Besanosaurus in an intermediate position between the subfamilies Cymbospondylinae and Shastasaurinae.
facts.quote: Besanosaurus was placed in an intermediate position between these two subfamilies by the analysis.

facts.statement: Sander found Besanosaurus to be the sister taxon of Cymbospondylus, with Shonisaurus being basal to both.
facts.quote: Sander found the three shastasaurids he included in his analysis to form a natural group, with Besanosaurus being the sister taxon of Cymbospondylus and Shonisaurus being basal to the two.

facts.statement: Maisch and Matzke found Besanosaurus to be the first taxon branching off from a grade leading to post-Triassic ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: they also found Motani's concept of Shastasauridae to be a grade leading up to the post-Triassic ichthyosaurs and their relatives, with Besanosaurus as the first of these taxa to branch off.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani (2003) placed Besanosaurus outside Merriamosauria and established the monotypic family Besanosauridae for it.
facts.quote: McGowan and Motani considered Besanosaurus to fall outside of Merriamosauria in 2003, and named a new monotypic family, Besanosauridae, to contain it.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus is the earliest known long-snouted diapsid reptile to reach a large body size.
facts.quote: Besanosaurus is the earliest known long-snouted diapsid that attained a large body size.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest large size in Besanosaurus allowed for diverse feeding techniques, acted as an anti-predator adaptation, and improved thermoregulation.
facts.quote: Bindellini listed many potential advantages of large size, including it allowing various feeding techniques, being an anti-predator adaptation, and resulting in more efficient thermoregulation.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Besanosaurus shows ankylosed, or pathologically fused, metatarsals.
facts.quote: The holotype of Besanosaurus exhibits ankylosed (pathologically fused) metatarsals.

facts.statement: A 2020 survey found shastasaurids like Besanosaurus showed more skeletal injuries than smaller mixosaurids but fewer than Cymbospondylus, suggesting they were preyed upon by larger animals.
facts.quote: A 2020 survey of ichthyosaurs from Monte San Giorgio by Judith Pardo-Pérez and colleagues found that shastasaurids like Besanosaurus were more likely to show skeletal injuries than the smaller mixosaurids, but showed less frequent injuries than Cymbospondylus, thought to have preyed upon larger animals.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus likely swam using an eel-like motion by undulating its entire flexible body from side to side.
facts.quote: Intermediate-grade ichthyosaurs likely used anguilliform (eel-like) or subcarangiform locomotion, swimming by undulating their entire body from side to side, owing to their long tails without strong bends and their long, flexible trunks.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus had predominantly single-headed ribs which resulted in a flexible body, unlike double-headed ribs found in other ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: The ribs of Besanosaurus were predominantly single-headed, with double-headed ribs limited to the neck. Since single-headed ribs are less firmly braced against the vertebrae than double-headed ribs, this would have resulted in a flexible body.

facts.statement: Researchers predicted Besanosaurus had a heterocercal tail fin with a much smaller upper lobe than the lower lobe, though no specimen preserves this fin.
facts.quote: While this fin is not preserved in any known specimen, Bindellini and colleagues predicted that it would have been heterocercal, with a much smaller upper lobe than lower.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus possessed particularly long limbs that helped stabilize the animal during swimming but were not used for propulsion.
facts.quote: The limbs of Besanosaurus were particularly long, which would have helped stabilize the animal while swimming, though they would not have been used for propulsion.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus had large coronoid processes and rough surangulars that would have anchored strong jaw musculature.
facts.quote: The large coronoid processes and rough, concave outer faces of the surangulars would have anchored strong jaw musculature.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus could not support a powerful bite, but its thin jaws allowed for rapid closing.
facts.quote: While the thin jaws of Besanosaurus would not have been able to support a powerful bite, Bindellini and colleagues noted that it could instead have allowed the jaws to rapidly close.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Besanosaurus may have consumed both fish and coleoids.
facts.quote: Bindellini and colleagues suggested that Besanosaurus may have consumed fish as well as coleoids.

facts.statement: In 2023, researchers interpreted the embryo found in the holotype as being oriented to be born tail first, similar to merriamosaurs.
facts.quote: In 2023, Miedema and colleagues interpretted the embryo as being oriented so that it would have been born tail first, as typical in merriamosaurs.

facts.statement: Some researchers debated whether the vertebrae found in the holotype were embryos or stomach contents of an immature mixosaurid, noting the vertebrae were the right size and more ossified than expected for an embryo.
facts.quote: Jiang and colleagues in 2020 were doubtful about the inability of Besanosaurus to have consumed mixosaurids, and argued that it could not be ruled out that the supposed embryos may be stomach contents instead, noting that the vertebrae were the right size for an immature mixosaurid, and were more ossified than would be expected in an embryo.

facts.statement: Besanosaurus dates to the latest Anisian and is the oldest definite shastasaurid genus.
facts.quote: The middle Besano Formation is also known as the N. secedensis Zone, and dates to the latest Anisian, meaning that Besanosaurus is the oldest definite shastasaurid genus.

facts.statement: The marine lagoon where Besanosaurus lived is estimated to have been 30 to 130 meters deep.
facts.quote: This lagoon is estimated to be 30 – 130 m deep.

facts.statement: The presence of terrestrial fossils like conifers and land-dwelling reptiles indicates the region was near land.
facts.quote: The presence of terrestrial fossils, such as conifers and land-dwelling reptiles indicates that the region would have been near land.

facts.statement: Fossils of Besanosaurus were first discovered in the spring of 1993 by volunteers of the Besano paleontological group at the "Sasso Caldo" quarry.
facts.quote: Los huesos fósiles del Besanosaurus fueron descubiertos por primera vez en el cantera "Sasso Caldo" en la primavera de 1993 por los voluntarios del grupo paleontológico de Besano

facts.statement: The Besanosaurus skeleton was prepared for 16,500 hours at the paleontological laboratory of the Museo Civico di Storia Naturale di Milano.
facts.quote: El esqueleto de Besanosaurus salió a la luz en el laboratorio paleontológico del Museo Civico di Storia Naturale di Milano después de 16.500 horas de preparación

facts.statement: 145 X-rays were required to detect the contents of the 38 stone slabs containing the Besanosaurus skeleton.
facts.quote: para detectar el contenido de las 38 losas de piedra en las que se distribuía el esqueleto, hicieron falta 145 radiografías

facts.statement: A silicone rubber matrix was created from the 38 stone slabs to produce a mold of the original Besanosaurus specimen.
facts.quote: Las 38 losas fueron re-ensambladas y una matriz de goma de silicona fue hecha, con lo que se obtuvo un molde del espécimen original

facts.statement: Besanosaurus was named by Dal Sasso and Pinna in 1996 and may be a member of the family Shastasauridae.
facts.quote: Este animal marino podría ser un miembro de la familia Shastasauridae, siendo nombrado por Dal Sasso y Pinna en 1996

facts.statement: Besanosaurus was a reptile about 6 meters long with a dolphin-like profile and a shape similar to the extinct Basilosaurus.
facts.quote: Besanosaurus era un reptil de cerca de 6 metros de longitud y tenía un perfil similar al de los delfines y forma similar al extinto Basilosaurus

facts.statement: Besanosaurus had a thin snout, small teeth, lacked a dorsal fin, and possessed a long, thin tail.
facts.quote: Tenía un hocico delgado, algunos dientes pequeños, carecía de aleta dorsal y poseía una cola larga y delgada

facts.statement: Besanosaurus likely swam by undulating its body like an eel, suggesting modest speed but capable of rapid acceleration and good maneuverability.
facts.quote: Parece haber sido un nadador que ondulaba su cuerpo de manera similar a una anguila, de modo que debió tener una modesta velocidad pero era capaz de una rápida aceleración y buena maniobrabilidad

facts.statement: Besanosaurus was a carnivore that primarily ate small fish, cephalopods, and other marine reptiles.
facts.quote: Besanosaurs era un carnívoro que comía mayormente peces pequeños, cefalópodos y otros reptiles marinos

facts.statement: Besanosaurus was likely ovoviviparous, meaning eggs incubated inside the body and young were born developed.
facts.quote: Probablemente era de reproducción ovovivípara, lo que significa que los huevos se incubaban dentro del cuerpo y así nacían ya desarrollados

facts.statement: The parent group of Besanosaurus is the family Besanosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Besanosauridae

facts.statement: The genus Besanosaurus was described by Dal Sasso & Pinna in 1996.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Dal Sasso & Pinna, 1996

facts.statement: The only known species of Besanosaurus is B. leptorhyncus.
facts.quote: subdivision: B. leptorhyncus

facts.statement: The fetus preserved in the Besanosaurus holotype shows evidence of palatine teeth.
facts.quote: reporting evidence of presence of palatine teeth
